meta.title: Colorado 2026 U.S. Senate: Abundance & Technology Analysis

scale.0: Strong evidence of opposition to the objective
scale.null: Unknown: no articulated position or no usable evidence

meta.method_note: Research was done through web search results that index the cited pages. Direct page retrieval was blocked in the research environment, so several entries rest on search excerpts of the linked page. Every entry links to the underlying page so a reader can check it. Entries marked Low confidence or 'unverified' should be checked before relying on them.

categories.name: Building abundance
categories.question: Does the candidate support increasing the supply of housing, infrastructure, and other essential goods and services?

categories.name: Energy abundance
categories.question: Does the candidate favor abundant, affordable, reliable energy, judged by likely effect on actual supply?

categories.name: Technological progress
categories.question: Does the candidate support the development and deployment of transformative technologies?

categories.name: Economic openness
categories.question: Does the candidate favor conditions that let new firms enter, invest, and compete?

categories.name: Pragmatism & execution
categories.question: Can the candidate translate objectives into effective policy?

candidates.name: John Hickenlooper
candidates.role: Incumbent U.S. Senator (since 2021); Governor of Colorado 2011–2019; Mayor of Denver 2003–2011

ballot.detail: Won the June 30, 2026 Democratic primary with 52.8% over state Sen. Julie Gonzales.

candidates.summary: The longest public record of the three. His record on supply is mostly concrete: a vote for the ROAD to Housing Act, authorship of transmission and geothermal bills, and a negotiating seat on the 2021 infrastructure law. Counter-evidence: he voted against the Ratepayer Protection Act, he favors liability-based AI rules that could slow deployment, and his position on nuclear power is not documented in the sources found.

candidates.name: Bob Chew
candidates.role: Co-founder and former CEO of CAI (Commissioning Agents, Inc.), an engineering consulting firm; Navy submarine officer

ballot.detail: CPR and the Colorado Forward Party identify him as the Forward Party nominee. Colorado Newsline's voter guide labels him Independent. He switched from the Republican Party to Forward in 2025. The Secretary of State's ballot listing could not be retrieved directly.

candidates.summary: No legislative record, so most evidence is stated intent and professional background. His statements lean toward supply: he says regulation delays homebuilding, that wind and solar alone cannot meet data-center demand, and that tariffs are a tax. He has few specific bills or mechanisms. On technology policy he has said almost nothing, so that score is Unknown.

candidates.name: Mark Baisley
candidates.role: Colorado State Senator, District 4 (since 2023); State Representative, HD 39 (2019–2023); 40-year IT career in aerospace and defense

ballot.detail: Only candidate to clear 30% at the April 11, 2026 Republican state assembly; unopposed in the June 30 primary.

candidates.summary: He has a state legislative record. He backs nuclear power and natural gas, and his record on technology bills is real but mixed: he voted for Colorado's AI Act and later led the bill that delayed it. Counter-evidence: he voted against Colorado's two main 2024 zoning-supply bills (ADUs and transit-oriented housing), he supports broad tariffs including replacing the income tax with tariff revenue, and he spoke at a 2022 election-conspiracy rally.

A.rationale: He voted for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bill aimed at regulatory barriers to building, and co-led the ePermit Act to digitize federal permitting. He also helped write the 2021 infrastructure law. These are supply-side actions. He is not a sponsor of the October 2026 Senate permitting package (S. 5653), and his vote on it is not yet known. That gap, and no record found of him pushing NEPA reform beyond the transmission provisions, keep the score at 3 rather than 4.

B.rationale: He sponsored BIG WIRES (interregional transmission), says much of the 2026 permitting deal's transmission title came from his bill, and co-led the Geo POWER Act for next-generation geothermal, which passed committee. As governor he brokered rules and deals that kept oil and gas drilling going under methane limits. Counter-evidence: he voted against advancing the Ratepayer Protection Act, arguing it was too weak to make data centers pay for grid costs. His nuclear position is undocumented in the sources found.

C.rationale: His support for research is strong: he was a CHIPS and Science Act conferee and chaired the subcommittee overseeing NSF, NIST and NASA. On deployment he is mixed. The VET AI Act sets voluntary standards, but he also favors third-party AI evaluators and making developers liable for harms, both of which add compliance cost. He opposed a federal moratorium on state AI laws, preferring national standards set by Congress.

D.rationale: He voted to end tariff emergencies on Canada and Brazil, which favors trade openness. He voted against the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1), which made full expensing of equipment and domestic R&D permanent; that is counter-evidence on investment incentives, though the bill also did many other things. No current skilled-immigration bill of his was found.

E.rationale: Two terms as governor and two as Denver mayor. Member of the G-22 group that wrote the 2021 infrastructure law. Several bipartisan bills enacted or advanced, including the ROAD to Housing Act and the geothermal bill. Ranked 27th of 98 senators on the Lugar Center Bipartisan Index for 2023.

A.rationale: His campaign calls Colorado's housing shortage a supply-and-demand problem and names government regulation that delays building as a cause. He also blames tariffs for higher construction costs. That is supply-side thinking, but it is general: no specific permitting, zoning or NEPA proposal was found, and he has no record to test it against.

B.rationale: He says data-center demand cannot be met by wind and solar alone, calls for an all-of-the-above strategy, and argues for a 'more measured' renewable transition, citing gas as roughly half the CO2 of coal. A Navy nuclear background is relevant context but not proof of policy. No specific bills or mechanisms (transmission, permitting, nuclear licensing) were found.

C.rationale: Unknown. The only technology statement found is a passing mention of AI as one tool for lowering health-care costs. His firm served life-sciences manufacturers and data centers, which is relevant context but is not a policy position.

D.rationale: He opposes tariffs ('a tax, plain and simple') and wants Congress to reclaim tariff authority. He blames regulation for higher costs. He would let each state set how many visas it accepts by category, which could widen or narrow skilled immigration. He would close capital-gains and estate-tax loopholes for the wealthy and put that revenue toward the debt, a tradeoff between a higher tax on capital and lower fiscal risk.

E.rationale: He has a verifiable private-sector record: he co-founded CAI in 1996 and grew it to about 750 employees and $135M before stepping down as CEO in 2022. He has no legislative record, which this analysis does not count against him. His policy proposals are general, and he has not explained how an unaffiliated senator would move them. The 2 reflects thin and mixed evidence, not a finding of poor performance.

A.rationale: His rhetoric is supply-side: he cites NAHB estimates that regulation adds about $131,734 to a new home. His votes cut the other way. He voted no on HB24-1152 (ADUs) and HB24-1313 (transit-oriented housing), Colorado's two main 2024 bills to loosen local zoning limits on supply. He voted yes on a housing-needs study. His main federal housing idea, a tax break for lenders to lower mortgage rates, subsidizes demand. A local-control principle may explain the no votes, but their effect on supply is still negative.

B.rationale: He sponsored SB25-139 to count nuclear as clean energy (killed in committee), tried to restore uranium mining in western Colorado, backs natural gas for AI-driven demand, and supports research on hydrogen and nuclear. Counter-evidence: he supports the 2025 reconciliation law, which phases out wind and solar credits, and broad tariffs that raise equipment costs. No transmission position was found.

C.rationale: He voted for Colorado's 2024 AI Act on final concurrence (35–0), then was the lead Senate sponsor of the 2025 bill delaying it. He says AI should be regulated 'lightly' through existing law, sponsored the Advanced Industries tax credit reauthorization, and pushes for aerospace jobs. He co-sponsored a neural-data privacy law, a modest new rule. Not documented: positions on federal research funding beyond energy research.

D.rationale: His tax and regulatory agenda favors investment: he supports the 2025 reconciliation law's expensing provisions and promises regulatory rollback. His trade stance is strongly against openness: he supports Trump's tariffs and wants tariff revenue to eventually replace the federal income tax. On immigration he accepts current legal admission levels and wants dangerous people deported. Pro-investment parts and protectionist parts roughly cancel.

E.rationale: Eight years as a minority-party legislator with several bipartisan laws, including the 2021 rulemaking-search law (98 of 100 legislators) and 2025 bills co-sponsored with Democrats. An aggregator counts 4 of 125 sponsored bills enacted (unverified). Counter-evidence: he spoke at a 2022 election-conspiracy rally and was pressed on it in the 2026 debate. That raises questions about judgment and credibility with colleagues.

hickenlooper.rationale: His record of cross-party lawmaking is measurable: the G-22 infrastructure group, ROAD to Housing, the VET AI Act with Capito, and Geo POWER with Daines. He ranked 27th of 98 on the Lugar Bipartisan Index (2023) but 62nd in 2021. He votes with his party on major party-line bills (IRA yes, H.R. 1 no). He voted to confirm some Trump Cabinet nominees and in October 2026 said he regrets it. That shows a willingness to break from his party, and also a reversal.

chew.rationale: No voting record, which this analysis does not count as partisanship. His stated positions mix both parties: he opposes tariffs and the Iran war's handling, and backs debt reduction and regulatory relief. He pledged not to support reconciliation bills, which pass on party-line votes. He backs open primaries and ranked-choice voting. Hickenlooper's campaign says Chew gave heavily to Republican senators before leaving the party. Chew says he gave to moderates in both parties. The donation record was not independently checked.

baisley.rationale: He has passed technical bills with Democrats: rulemaking search with Titone, neural-data privacy with Priola and Kipp, and 2025 bills with Mullica, Marchman and Snyder. He describes himself as a contrarian voter. He criticized the Trump administration's move of Space Command. But he spoke at a 2022 election-conspiracy rally, at first backed GOP amendments endorsing election-fraud claims before calling that a mistake, and backs most of the Trump agenda, including tariffs and H.R. 1.

evidence.claim: Voted for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
evidence.summary: Hickenlooper's office says he voted to pass the bill and to advance the negotiated version. CBS reported Senate approval 85–5. Coverage describes the bill as cutting red tape and administrative barriers to housing construction. Secondary sources disagree on dates and on final enactment details.
evidence.source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper (corroborated by CBS News)
evidence.interpretation: A vote for a bipartisan bill aimed at regulatory barriers to supply. One of 85 yes votes, so it shows alignment more than leadership.

evidence.claim: Co-led the bipartisan ePermit Act
evidence.summary: Introduced February 2026; would replace paper applications and siloed federal permitting with an interactive online platform.
evidence.interpretation: Process reform that could shorten review timelines. Introduction only; no enactment found.

evidence.claim: Member of the G-22 bipartisan group that wrote the 2021 infrastructure law
evidence.summary: One of 22 senators who negotiated the ~$1.2T Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act; it passed the Senate 69–30 in August 2021 with 19 Republican votes. His office says it included his RECHARGE Act.
evidence.interpretation: Direct infrastructure funding and bipartisan negotiation. Spending is not the same as faster building, but the law did fund physical capacity.

evidence.claim: Sponsored the BIG WIRES Act (S. 2827)
evidence.summary: Would require each FERC planning region to be able to transfer a set share of peak load to neighbors (the lesser of 30% of peak load or peak transmission plus 15%). A Columbia CGEP analysis estimated it would more than double interregional transfer capacity to 191 GW in ten years.
evidence.interpretation: Targets a real constraint: transmission is a bottleneck for every kind of generation. Introduced, not enacted.

evidence.claim: Says much of the 2026 Senate permitting deal began as his transmission bill
evidence.summary: S. 5653 (introduced Sept. 30, 2026 by Capito, Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich) revises NEPA, CWA and ESA processes and gives FERC permitting authority for transmission in the public interest. Hickenlooper is not a sponsor. A floor vote is expected after the election. No public statement of how he will vote was found.
evidence.legislation: S. 5653, Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
evidence.interpretation: His claim of influence is plausible given BIG WIRES, but his actual vote is not yet known. It is the most important pending test of his permitting stance.

evidence.claim: Co-led the Geo POWER Act with Sen. Daines; passed Energy committee
evidence.summary: Introduced March 17, 2026. Gives DOE financing tools and milestone-based investments for next-generation geothermal demonstrations; his office describes about $800M. Passed the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee as amended.
evidence.source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper; GovInfo S. 4116
evidence.interpretation: Supports firm, around-the-clock clean power. Public money for demonstrations is a subsidy, but aimed at new supply.

evidence.claim: Voted against advancing the Ratepayer Protection Act
evidence.summary: After the House passed it 417–3, the bill failed Senate cloture 57–43. Hickenlooper voted no, calling it inadequate: it asks states to consider ratepayer protections but does not require them. He argues data centers should pay grid costs and meet local water and noise standards.
evidence.source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper; CBS News
evidence.interpretation: Contrary evidence on its face, since he blocked a near-unanimous House bill. His stated reason is cost allocation, not limiting supply, but adding local standards could slow data-center buildout.

evidence.claim: As governor, brokered methane rules and a 2014 deal that kept anti-fracking measures off the ballot
evidence.summary: In 2013–14 Colorado became the first state to limit methane from oil and gas production, under rules written jointly by producers and the Environmental Defense Fund. In August 2014 he brokered a deal that withdrew four ballot measures and set up a task force.
evidence.interpretation: Executive record of keeping gas supply going while adding environmental rules. Shows a willingness to break with his party's left on energy.

evidence.claim: Position on nuclear and advanced reactors: unknown
evidence.summary: The ADVANCE Act passed the Senate 88–2 on June 18, 2024; only Markey and Sanders voted no and ten senators did not vote. No source found states Hickenlooper's individual vote or a statement from him on advanced reactors.
evidence.interpretation: He was not one of the two no votes, but he may have been among the ten who did not vote. Unverified; check Senate roll call.

evidence.claim: Voted for the Inflation Reduction Act
evidence.summary: The IRA passed the Senate 51–50 in August 2022 with all Democrats voting yes. It created long-term tax credits for wind, solar, storage, nuclear and other generation.
evidence.interpretation: Subsidies that expanded generation supply. Party-line vote, so it says little about independence.

evidence.claim: CHIPS and Science Act conferee and science-subcommittee chair
evidence.summary: As chair of the Commerce Committee's Space and Science Subcommittee he oversaw NSF, NIST, NASA and OSTP. He sat on the conference committee and presided over the final Senate vote. The law includes semiconductor incentives and advanced-nuclear R&D provisions.
evidence.source: Office of Sen. Hickenlooper; Congress.gov H.R. 4346
evidence.interpretation: Strong evidence of support for research and domestic manufacturing.

evidence.claim: Co-led the VET AI Act with Sen. Capito
evidence.summary: S. 2615 directs NIST to develop voluntary specifications for third-party evaluators who verify AI developers' testing and risk-management claims. Reintroduced July 31, 2025.
evidence.interpretation: Voluntary standards are light-touch and could build trust that helps adoption.

evidence.claim: Wants third-party AI evaluators, developer liability for damages, and data-privacy protections
evidence.summary: Colorado Sun candidate guide: he would like third-party evaluators overseeing AI work, assurances that developers can be sued for damages their products cause, and protections for private data.
evidence.interpretation: Liability and oversight have intended consumer benefits but raise deployment costs and legal uncertainty, especially for smaller developers.

evidence.claim: Opposed a 10-year federal moratorium on state AI laws; wants Congress to set national standards
evidence.summary: His office predicted the moratorium would be stripped from H.R. 1. The Senate struck it 99–1 on July 1, 2025 (Blackburn amendment). Only Sen. Tillis voted no, which implies Hickenlooper voted to strip it.
evidence.interpretation: Keeps states able to regulate AI, a patchwork that raises compliance costs, while saying he prefers federal standards. His vote is inferred from the 99–1 tally.

evidence.claim: Passed a bipartisan quantum development investment bill through Commerce Committee
evidence.summary: His office reports Commerce Committee passage of a bipartisan quantum investment bill. The bill number and date were not captured in the sources found.
evidence.interpretation: Supports research funding. Committee stage only.

evidence.claim: Voted to terminate the national emergency used for tariffs on Canada
evidence.summary: Senate roll call 160 (April 2, 2025), S.J.Res. 37; Hickenlooper voted Yea. Four Republicans joined Democrats.
evidence.interpretation: Supports trade openness and lower input costs.

evidence.claim: Voted to end 50% tariffs on Brazil
evidence.summary: His office says he voted with all Democrats and five Republicans to end the Brazil tariffs.
evidence.legislation: Joint resolution on Brazil tariff emergency
evidence.interpretation: Consistent with H16.

evidence.claim: Voted against the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1)
evidence.summary: H.R. 1 passed the Senate 51–50 on July 1, 2025 with every Democrat opposed. It made full expensing for equipment and domestic R&D permanent, cut Medicaid, and phased out wind and solar credits.
evidence.legislation: H.R. 1 (119th), One Big Beautiful Bill Act
evidence.interpretation: Counter-evidence on investment incentives (expensing), though his no vote also reflected the bill's energy-credit and health cuts. A large omnibus vote is a weak signal on any one issue.

evidence.claim: Ranked 27th of 98 senators on the Lugar Center Bipartisan Index (2023); 62nd in 2021
evidence.summary: The index measures how often a member's bills attract cosponsors from the other party and how often they cosponsor the other party's bills. 2023 score 0.41157.
evidence.interpretation: Above the Senate median recently. Measures cosponsorship, not votes or results.

evidence.claim: Governor 2011–2019; Denver mayor 2003–2011; founded a brewpub business
evidence.summary: Long executive record at city and state level before entering the Senate in 2021.
evidence.interpretation: Extensive administrative experience. Not by itself proof of policy alignment.

evidence.claim: Says he now regrets voting to confirm Trump Cabinet nominees
evidence.summary: In the Oct. 14, 2026 9NEWS debate he said his earlier strategy of supporting some nominees to 'reduce the damage' for Colorado did not work.
evidence.interpretation: Shows he once broke with his party on confirmations, and that he now says he would not.

evidence.claim: Won the Democratic primary 52.8% over progressive state Sen. Julie Gonzales
evidence.summary: A narrow primary win against a challenger from his party's left.
evidence.interpretation: Context: he is positioned toward the center of his party.

evidence.claim: Co-founded CAI (Commissioning Agents, Inc.) in 1996; CEO until 2022
evidence.summary: CAI serves life-sciences, data-center and industrial manufacturers. The succession announcement credits him with growing it to a $135M global firm with 750 employees. He stayed on as board chair and chief innovation officer. Campaign coverage calls it employee-owned; that detail was not independently confirmed.
evidence.interpretation: Real record of building and running a technical firm. Relevant to execution; not proof of policy skill.

evidence.claim: Navy submarine officer with a nuclear engineering background
evidence.summary: CPR reports he has a nuclear engineering background from Navy service.
evidence.interpretation: Relevant context for nuclear policy, but no explicit nuclear policy found.

evidence.claim: Former Republican; switched to the Forward Party in 2025
evidence.summary: CPR's voter guide identifies him as the Forward Party nominee. He calls his campaign independent. He says the Forward Party has no policy positions.
evidence.interpretation: Ballot status confirmed. Party switch is recent.

evidence.claim: Calls the housing shortage a supply-and-demand problem worsened by regulation that delays building
evidence.summary: His issues page lists mortgage rates, construction costs and government regulation that delays building more homes as causes.
evidence.interpretation: Correct supply-side diagnosis, with no specific mechanism.

evidence.claim: Blames tariffs and regulations for higher home-building costs; ties the national debt to mortgage rates
evidence.summary: In CPR's voter guide he attributed most affordability problems to government actions such as tariffs and regulations that raise building costs, and said he has a 'credible plan' on the debt.
evidence.interpretation: Points to input costs and capital costs, both supply-side.

evidence.claim: Says data-center demand cannot be met by wind and solar alone; backs an all-of-the-above strategy
evidence.summary: His issues page says large digital demand cannot possibly be met by wind and solar alone and calls for an all-of-the-above strategy with heavy reliance on other sources. The excerpt found did not name those sources.
evidence.interpretation: Technology-neutral, supply-focused framing. No mechanism given.

evidence.claim: Calls for a 'more measured' renewable transition; cites gas at roughly half of coal's CO2
evidence.summary: In the CPR interview he also said Colorado pays the highest retail electricity rates of its neighboring states.
evidence.interpretation: Weighs reliability and cost. Mostly about Colorado policy, with less federal detail.

evidence.claim: Lists restoring American energy dominance among his goals
evidence.summary: Reported in the Colorado Newsline voter guide citing his website.
evidence.interpretation: Slogan-level.

evidence.claim: No technology platform found; AI mentioned only as a health-care cost tool
evidence.summary: In the CPR interview he listed price transparency, competition and greater use of technology, 'including that dreaded word AI', as parts of health-care cost reform.
evidence.interpretation: Mildly positive toward deployment, but not enough to score.

evidence.claim: 'Tariffs are a tax, plain and simple'; wants Congress to reassert tariff authority
evidence.summary: His site says tariffs raise consumer prices, create uncertainty for small businesses, and punish domestic exporters.
evidence.interpretation: Clear pro-trade position with a constitutional-process element.

evidence.claim: Would let each state decide how many visas it accepts in each category
evidence.summary: Confirmed in the CPR interview and described in CPR's voter guide.
evidence.interpretation: New idea. It could raise skilled admissions in states that want talent, or lower them elsewhere. Net effect is uncertain.

evidence.claim: Close capital-gains and estate-tax loopholes for the ultra-wealthy; earmark revenue for debt reduction and entitlement solvency
evidence.summary: His top issue is the national debt (more than $40 trillion), which he calls 'a ticking time bomb.'
evidence.interpretation: Higher tax on inherited capital, against lower fiscal risk and interest rates. The capital-formation effect depends on design.

evidence.claim: Focus enforcement on violent criminals and cartel traffickers, not peaceful immigrants who contribute to the economy
evidence.summary: Stated on his campaign site.
evidence.interpretation: Labor-supply friendly.

evidence.claim: Would not support reconciliation bills; calls bipartisanship the best long-term approach
evidence.summary: Stated in CPR's voter guide.
evidence.interpretation: A pro-consensus pledge. It would also rule out the main way recent Congresses have passed tax and energy law, which could limit what he can deliver.

evidence.claim: Largely self-funded (more than $1M of his own money; $1.5M ad expansion); excluded from 9NEWS debate
evidence.summary: Colorado Politics reports the self-funding and ad buys. He did not meet 9NEWS's 15% polling threshold. A Substack interview says he was not allowed to take part in the Club 20 debate.
evidence.interpretation: Context on viability. It does not measure governing ability.

evidence.claim: Hickenlooper campaign: he donated heavily to GOP senators including Susan Collins. Chew: he gave to moderates of both parties
evidence.summary: Both claims come from the campaigns. The FEC donation record was not checked independently for this analysis.
evidence.interpretation: Unverified. Giving to Collins, a moderate, fits either story.

evidence.claim: Supports open primaries and ranked-choice voting
evidence.summary: Reported by Smarter.vote and IVN as part of his platform.
evidence.interpretation: Reforms meant to reduce partisan incentives.

evidence.claim: Criticized President Trump's handling of the war in Iran despite his Republican past
evidence.summary: Reported by CPR.
evidence.interpretation: Breaks with his former party on a major issue.

evidence.claim: Says the Forward Party has no policy positions
evidence.summary: Said in the CPR interview.
evidence.interpretation: His positions are his own. There is no party caucus or platform to lean on.

evidence.claim: Voted NO on HB24-1313 (Housing in Transit-Oriented Communities)
evidence.summary: Official Senate third-reading record, May 7, 2024: passed 19–15, Baisley No. The bill set housing-capacity goals near transit for larger cities.
evidence.interpretation: A vote against the state's main density-near-transit supply bill. It may reflect a local-control principle, but the effect on supply is negative.

evidence.claim: Voted NO on HB24-1152 (Accessory Dwelling Units)
evidence.summary: Official Senate third-reading record, May 6, 2024: passed 20–15, Baisley No. He voted yes on a same-day amendment that passed 35–0.
evidence.interpretation: ADU legalization is one of the most direct supply reforms available. Voting no runs against the stated objective.

evidence.claim: Voted YES on SB24-174 (statewide housing-needs assessment)
evidence.summary: Passed the Senate 32–1 on April 19, 2024 and the concurrence 35–0, with Baisley voting yes. It requires a statewide needs assessment and local grants.
evidence.interpretation: A study and planning bill. It does not change rules that limit building.

evidence.claim: Cites NAHB: regulatory costs up ~40% in five years, adding ~$131,734 to a new home; blames 'unelected bureaucrats'
evidence.summary: Reported by The Center Square from his campaign materials.
evidence.interpretation: Supply-side diagnosis aimed at federal rules. It sits in tension with his state votes on zoning.

evidence.claim: Proposes tax breaks for lenders tied to the 10-year Treasury yield to lower mortgage rates
evidence.summary: Stated in CPR's voter guide, along with a national fix for property taxes.
evidence.interpretation: Subsidizes demand. Without more supply, cheaper credit tends to push prices up.

evidence.claim: Prime sponsor of SB25-139, which would have counted nuclear as a clean energy resource
evidence.summary: Introduced Feb. 5, 2025; postponed indefinitely by the Senate State, Veterans & Military Affairs Committee on March 4, 2025.
evidence.interpretation: Concrete pro-nuclear effort. It did not pass.

evidence.claim: Pursued legislation to restore uranium mining in western Colorado (unsuccessful)
evidence.summary: Highlighted in the Colorado Sun candidate guide. Bill number not identified.
evidence.interpretation: Fuel-supply side of nuclear. Unverified at the bill level.

evidence.claim: Would keep using carbon-emitting sources; sees natural gas meeting AI-driven demand; backs government research on hydrogen and nuclear
evidence.summary: From CPR's voter guide and the Colorado Sun candidate guide. He also says he supports efforts to minimize human impact on the climate.
evidence.source: Colorado Public Radio voter guide; The Colorado Sun
evidence.interpretation: Favors firm supply. Less clear on renewables, storage and transmission.

evidence.claim: Pledges 'American energy dominance', energy independence, and regulatory rollback
evidence.summary: Campaign pledge reported by Colorado Politics and Colorado Newsline.
evidence.interpretation: Slogan-level.

evidence.claim: Supports the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1)
evidence.summary: CPR reports he supports both the GOP spending bill and Trump's tariffs. H.R. 1 phased out wind and solar credits and made full expensing permanent.
evidence.interpretation: Fewer subsidies may slow near-term wind and solar buildout, while expensing helps capital investment.

evidence.claim: Voted YES on final concurrence of the Colorado AI Act (SB24-205)
evidence.summary: Official record, May 8, 2024: 35–0, Baisley Yes. One aggregator lists him as a primary sponsor; the official sponsor list names Rodriguez, Titone and Rutinel.
evidence.interpretation: He supported the nation's first broad state AI-discrimination law, which industry widely criticized as burdensome. Counter-evidence to his 'regulate lightly' stance.

evidence.claim: Lead Senate sponsor of SB25B-004, delaying the AI Act to June 30, 2026
evidence.summary: Signed Aug. 28, 2025 in a special session. In May 2026 the legislature repealed and replaced the Act with a disclosure-based framework.
evidence.interpretation: Reduced near-term compliance burden on AI deployers.

evidence.claim: Co-sponsored HB24-1058 adding neural and biological data to the Colorado Privacy Act
evidence.summary: Bipartisan sponsors: Reps. Kipp and Soper; Sens. Priola and Baisley. Signed by Gov. Polis.
evidence.interpretation: A narrow privacy rule for neurotech. Modest compliance cost; also shows bipartisan work.

evidence.claim: Says AI should be regulated 'lightly', mainly by applying existing laws, with protections against discrimination and deepfakes
evidence.summary: Colorado Sun candidate guide and debate coverage.
evidence.interpretation: Deployment-friendly stance.

evidence.claim: Calls the Space Command move to Alabama political; would fight for aerospace jobs
evidence.summary: Said in the CPR interview. He also blamed Hickenlooper for not keeping Space Command in Colorado.
evidence.interpretation: Supports the aerospace sector. Also a rare break with the Trump administration.

evidence.claim: Senate sponsor of HB25-1157, reauthorizing Colorado's Advanced Industries tax credit
evidence.summary: Co-sponsored with Democratic Sen. Snyder; signed by the governor.
evidence.interpretation: Supports investment in advanced industries, including aerospace, bioscience and cleantech.

evidence.claim: Defends Trump's tariffs; wants tariff revenue to eventually replace the federal income tax
evidence.summary: Said in the CPR interview.
evidence.interpretation: Replacing income-tax revenue would require very high, broad tariffs, raising input costs and inviting retaliation against exporters.

evidence.claim: Deport dangerous immigrants; vetted legal immigrants can stay; ~1M legal admissions a year is small enough to assimilate
evidence.summary: CPR voter guide.
evidence.interpretation: Accepts current legal levels. No position found on skilled-visa expansion.

evidence.claim: Co-sponsored HB21-1230 (agency rulemaking search) with Democrat Brianna Titone; 98 of 100 legislators supported it
evidence.summary: Signed in July 2021. Baisley said people with different social views can readily agree on technical problems.
evidence.interpretation: Practical, transparency-minded lawmaking across party lines.

evidence.claim: About 125 bills sponsored, 4 enacted (aggregator count)
evidence.summary: Third-party tracker figure, not checked against official records. Also lists a nuclear workforce bill as passed (unverified).
evidence.interpretation: A low enactment rate is common for minority-party members. Treat as unverified.

evidence.claim: Featured speaker at an April 2022 Capitol rally with Mike Lindell and Tina Peters
evidence.summary: Reported by States Newsroom. In the Oct. 14, 2026 9NEWS debate, moderator Kyle Clark pressed him on his past embrace of election-rigging claims.
evidence.interpretation: Evidence of ideological rigidity. Damages cross-party trust.

evidence.claim: Said he made a mistake supporting GOP amendments endorsing election-fraud claims
evidence.summary: In early 2022 he told a radio interviewer his votes for those House amendments were a mistake.
evidence.interpretation: A partial walk-back, followed months later by the rally appearance (B21).

evidence.claim: 2025 laws co-sponsored with Democrats: HB25-1195 (with Mullica) and HB25-1053 (with Marchman)
evidence.summary: HB25-1195: first-responder voter-record confidentiality. HB25-1053: landowner immunity for emergency access. Both signed.
evidence.interpretation: Steady cross-party work on narrow bills.
